entries.note: Borrowed from French; it was originally the name of a spiced goose stew.
From French, literally 'rotten pot'; it was originally the name of a stew.
From a French word meaning to make merry and eat a lot; it was also the name of a hash.
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[genteel]], [[gentile]] and [[jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[gentle]], [[gentile]] and [[jaunty]].
One of four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice'; the others are [[gentle]], [[genteel]] and [[jaunty]].
Rob's favourite of the four English borrowings of French [[gentil]], 'nice', alongside [[gentle]], [[genteel]] and [[gentile]].
Shakespeare turned the noun into a verb: to uncle someone.
Shakespeare is the first recorded written user of 'to ghost' as a verb, which seems surprisingly modern.
An acronym for the unwritten order of adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose. That's why 'big old black' sounds right.

entries.translation: a thing high up in the air
entries.note: From Greek meteoron; in the 15th century any visible atmospheric phenomenon counted, from wind and rain to rainbows, auroras and lightning.
Weather science is named after [[meteor]] in its old sense of any atmospheric phenomenon, despite not obviously involving meteors.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
One of the many British regional words for types of rain.
A Scottish word in the hosts' list of regional rain words; Jess thinks it generally means gross.
Literally 'a thing that's running': like the [[current]] of a river, it comes from Latin currentia, meaning running.
From German Kupfernickel, 'copper goblin' or 'copper devil'. Miners gave it that name because the copper-coloured ore yielded no copper, and Nickel was a nickname for the devil.
Literally 'the devil's fart bread', containing the same devil nickname as [[nickel]]; Jess mentions it at every opportunity.
Meant a ship's steersman in the 1500s. It comes from a medieval Greek word for rudder that shares a root with the foot-related ped- words, probably comparing a rudder to a foot.
Borrowed from French aile, 'wing', so planes have wings inside; its silent s was added to match [[isle]].
Its silent s is only there to match the silent s in [[island]], and it in turn lent the s to [[aisle]].
Samuel Johnson's 1755 dictionary defined a politician as a man of artifice, one of deep contrivance.
Johnson defined it as 'not exhilarating, not delightful', with the self-referential example 'to make dictionaries is dull work'.
Johnson famously defined a lexicographer, a dictionary writer, as a harmless drudge.
Originally a trademarked name for a small medicine tablet. It then meant compressed news and small papers with short articles, and only later sensationalized news.
An overly elaborate synonym journalists use to avoid repeating a word; the name itself is one such way of referring to a crocodile.
A [[knobbly monster]] journalists used to avoid repeating the word badger.
A [[knobbly monster]] used for Darth Vader.
Named by Erik the Red to attract others to settle there, even though it is clearly not green.
Named by Flóki Vilgerðarson to scare people off, because he thought it a terrible place to settle.
Jacques Cartier recorded kanata for one specific area, not the whole territory. A popular myth derives it from Spanish or Portuguese for 'nothing here'.
A popular myth says it comes from a phrase meaning 'I don't know', said when someone asked what the animal was.
The bird-hipped dinosaurs. Surprisingly, it was the lizard-hipped [[saurischian|saurischians]], not these, that became birds.
The lizard-hipped dinosaurs; they, not the bird-hipped [[ornithischian|ornithischians]], are the ones that became birds.
Named in 1877 by Othniel Charles Marsh from Greek stegos 'roof' and sauros 'lizard'. He thought its plates lay flat like shingles.
Its -dom is unrelated to dominion but related to [[doom]]: Old English dom meant a law or judgment, so a kingdom is a territory defined by decree.
Old English dom meant a law, decree or judgment, extended to a decision determining fate or destiny; it is also the -dom in [[kingdom]].
An old word for a judge, from [[doom]] in its sense of judgment; Jess thinks it a great name.
William the Conqueror's compendious volume charting who owned what land, brought up in connection with [[doom]].
The Egyptian word means 'great house' and originally referred to the building the ruler lived in rather than the office.
Originally described a well-fed horse, energetic from its beans and more likely to win a race; nothing to do with feeding people beans.
Compared only for about a century; from the 1670s people compared apples to oysters instead, as in 'as like as an apple to an oyster'.
Hides a [[deer]]: a 'wild-deer-ness' was a place characterized by the presence of wild beasts.
In Old English it meant any wild quadruped, not only a deer; it survives in the middle of [[wilderness]].
From Latin contra 'against', implying what lies in front of you; it has nothing to do with borders.
Thought to come from French poupée 'doll', the same word that gives [[puppet]] and [[poppet]].
From the same French word for doll as [[puppy]].
Also from French poupée 'doll', like [[puppy]] and [[puppet]]; a cute little thing you love.
The classic dog name comes from Latin fidus, 'faithful', and is related to [[fidelity]]. In the 1940s a famous Italian dog named Fido waited daily at a bus stop.
First recorded with this spelling in Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, modelled on a similar Hebrew name of a minor biblical figure.
Typically a surname before Shakespeare used it in The Tempest.
Possibly adapted from a Welsh name or French-inspired, but only popularized by Shakespeare's King Lear.
Sometimes credited to Shakespeare, though it was already popular on the Continent; he may have been among the first to give it to a character.
The same name as [[Seamus]], in the vocative form used to address him. English speakers overheard it and took it for a separate name.
[[Hamish]] and [[Seamus]] are both forms of James, which is itself also [[Jacob]].
A word lent to another language and later borrowed back, like [[tennis]] and [[artichoke]].
From French tenez, 'hold, take', said when hitting the ball. It's a [[boomerang word]]: French borrowed tennis back, even calling a tennis shoe a tennis.
Named because it was played on foot rather than on horseback, unlike 1700s gentlemen's sports, not because of kicking.
Short for association football; a British English term.
The only country named after a real historical woman, St Lucy of Syracuse; French sailors named it after arriving on her feast day.
Joseph Heller's novel was originally Catch-18, changed because another book with 18 in the title, Mila 18, was coming out.
Originally meant 'scratch', for runic writing. It is unique among Germanic languages, whose words relate to [[scribe]], which also means scratch.
A school of fish is borrowed from Middle Dutch and related to [[shoal]]. It is unrelated to the educational school, whose basic sense is leisure.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
One of several nautical words English got from Dutch.
In Thomas Harman's 1500s rogue literature, a former soldier who harasses people.
Thomas Harman's 1500s term for a horse thief.
Thomas Harman's 1500s term for someone who fakes seizures or medical emergencies to rob people.

entries.term: hoddy-doddy, all arse and no body
entries.note: Francis Grose's 18th-century Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue records it as London slang for a clumsy person.
From Air Force slang, picturing a loop-the-loop going wrong.
The word for something pear-shaped, which Rob looked up while discussing [[go pear-shaped]].
Its loop, spelled loupe in Middle English, is unrelated to other loops. It meant a narrow vertical slit in a fortification that archers and musketeers fired through.
Probably coined in 1995 by Puerto Rican comedian Silverio Pérez. Properly chupacabras, 'goats-sucker'; English misread the final s as a plural.
Latin for 'I will please', from the opening of a prayer and later applied to drugs; its opposite is [[nocebo]].
The opposite of [[placebo]], as in the nocebo effect. It sounds made up, but it's genuine Latin for 'I will cause harm'.
Thought to mean 'dry', from a Germanic seafaring phrase for dry goods or barrels. It covered spices, herbs and medicines, then narrowed to apothecary wares.
A rebracketing of [[cybernetics]]: in Greek kybernetes, 'steersman', the n belongs with kyber, so it should really be 'cybern'.
First used in 1993, when Richard Depew accidentally posted one message 200 times to Usenet. It references the Monty Python sketch of Vikings singing 'spam'.
Once just meant a machine operator. The Pinkerton agency, unpopular after violent strikebreaking, started calling its detectives operatives as a more neutral term.
A French rendering of a Miami-Illinois word for pungent wild garlic, leeks and ramps. It was also used for skunks, and its root is said to mean urinate.
-chester means fort, like -caster and -cester. Man- shares an ancient root with [[mammal]] and [[mammary]], giving 'fort at the breast-shaped hill'.
Xerox fought generic use of its name for photocopiers, with slogans like 'when you use Xerox the way you use aspirin, we get a headache'.
From an Italian word for a bobbin or small distaff used in spinning; it applies to both space and firework rockets.
Long meant a dart or missile. The vehicle sense, and later space shuttle, comes from weaving, where the shuttle goes back and forth.
A word that should theoretically exist but doesn't, such as 'groomal' beside [[bridal]].
Originally a compound noun, bride-ale, meaning a party with ale for a bride. That is why there's no 'groomal'.
A Middle English harvest party, one of several -ale party words like the bride-ale behind [[bridal]].
English has no word for someone who is alive, since 'liver' would sound and be spelled the same as the organ.
Jess's proposed word to fill the [[lexical gap]] for someone who is not a virgin but hasn't had a lot of sex.
A historical term for sex, recorded centuries ago.
'Playing hot cockles' is a historical term for sex.
'Being at the service of Venus' is a historical term for sex.
From the Greek for porch, because its founder Zeno lectured on a decorated porch at the Agora in Athens.
From Greek kynikos, 'doglike'. It may refer to the coarse lifestyle of Antisthenes' followers, or to the Cynosarges ('grey dog'), where he taught.
Caleb Bradham sold it from 1893 as Brad's Drink. He renamed it Pepsi-Cola in 1898 because it was advertised to relieve dyspepsia.
Originally called BackRub, because the system checked backlinks to estimate a site's importance.
Gibberish chosen by Reuben and Rose Mattus in the Bronx to sound foreign, vaguely Danish; it doesn't actually mean anything.
A variant of [[curse]] that lost its r through assimilatory loss, the same process behind [[ass]] from [[arse]] and [[bust]] from [[burst]].
A variant of [[arse]] through the same sound loss that gives [[cuss]] from [[curse]].
A variant of [[burst]] through the same sound loss that gives [[cuss]] from [[curse]].
John McWhorter calls mocking someone who misuses whom the last acceptable classism, like rapping them with a cane in 1885.
A starter in British English but the main dish in North America. Wartime and Depression-era restaurants repositioned entrées as filling enough to replace the main course.
Short for 's-Gravenhage, 'the count's hedge', after the hedge around the hunting grounds there.
Given by the conquering Fatimid caliph in the 10th century. Medieval writers linked it to an Arabic name for Mars, 'the victorious star'.
In the late 16th century, a horse race: riders followed a leader's erratic course in a staggered pattern resembling flying wild geese.
Its first member may be Lord Cholmondeley, who bet Lord Derby in 1785 he could have sex in a balloon. The term predates planes flying a mile high.
A sentence, literally 'pull me up'. Possibly named because its coffee perks you up, though some speculate it was invented at a brothel.
Named after maître d' Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who improvised them in 1943 at Mexico's Victory Club for US officers' wives.
From Latin lira, 'furrow'; the verb meant to go off the furrow, the classical equivalent of [[off the rails]].
Freud wrote in German and called it das Es, 'the it'; the Latin term id is not his.
Freud, writing in German, called it das Ich, 'the I', rather than the Latin ego.
Freud, writing in German, called it das Über-Ich, 'the over-I' or 'super-I', rather than the Latin superego.
From Arabic for 'the die' via French. It named a dice game before meaning risk, and pronouncing the h is an overcorrection.
From Arabic via Italian and Spanish, with letter-salad spellings. A [[boomerang word]]: Levantine Arabic borrowed it back as ardishawki, folk-etymologized as 'earthy thorny'.
Its Jerusalem is just Italian girasole, 'sunflower', and it isn't really an [[artichoke]].
From Zanni, the servant clown of commedia dell'arte, a Venetian form of Gianni, pet form of Giovanni; it was a noun before an adjective.
From a French word meaning 'to stuff'. Farces were comic relief rammed in to pad out serious productions, for example during set changes.
The ancient letter behind [[F]], [[U]], [[V]], [[W]] and Y looked most like Y, a fork on a stick. Y reflects the Greek use, hence 'Greek I'.
Descends from the same fork-shaped ancient letter as [[U]], [[V]], [[W]] and [[Y]], with the fork leaned over.
Originally the same letter as [[V]]; both share one ancient ancestor with [[F]], [[W]] and [[Y]].
The ancient fork-shaped letter with its stick shortened; the same letter as [[U]], and related to [[F]], [[W]] and [[Y]].
Just a repeated [[U]] or [[V]], sharing one ancient ancestor with [[F]] and [[Y]].
From Spanish mestengo, 'stray animal'. That comes from the Mesta, a livestock owners' council said to mean 'mixed', perhaps for dividing mixed strays; not mixed breeds.
From Spanish, meaning someone who is affectionate about a thing rather than an expert; directly related to [[affectionate]].
The band spelled it L-E-D so people wouldn't read it as 'Lead Zeppelin'.
Juke is from a Wolof and Gullah word for rowdy. Coin-operated jukeboxes were named after [[juke joint|juke joints]], where Black people in the southeastern US danced, drank and gambled.
A word that looks like a word in another language but means something different, like [[empathy]] and its Modern Greek lookalike.
From Greek empatheia, 'passion, inner feeling'. It's a [[false friend]] of Modern Greek empatheia, which means animosity or malevolence.
An English-looking German [[false friend]] meaning a vintage car.
In German not a car but a projector; a [[false friend]].
In German, a backpack with one strap; a [[false friend]].
German for a mobile phone. It borrows an English word that doesn't exist in this sense; the German for hand is simply Hand.
Slang made by reversing words, as in [[yob]] from boy and [[slop]] from police; probably also the source of [[moniker]].
Most likely [[back slang]] for [[nickname]], which reversed comes out close to moniker, though moniker oddly sounds more formal.
From 'an ekename', which became 'a nickname'; reversed in [[back slang]], it probably gave [[moniker]].
[[back slang]] for boy.
[[back slang]] for police.
Ben Zimmer traces it to Aretha Franklin's 1967 'Respect', where she sings 'give me my propers'. It was shortened in Black slang; Otis Redding's version lacks the line.
From Old French, literally 'made of hemp', so it's related to [[cannabis]] and practically a doublet of it.
A type of canvas whose 'duck' comes from a Dutch word for cloth; it gave [[duct tape]] its original name.
Began as a non-adhesive strip of [[cotton duck]] cloth named after the fabric. The name later passed to the plastic-coated adhesive tape WWII soldiers used.
Borrowed from Dutch ezel, 'donkey'; Jess compares it to the animals in [[clothes horse]] and [[sawhorse]].
A contraction of Old Norse 'at do', since Norse used at instead of to for infinitives. So ado means much the same as a [[to-do]].
The Old English counterpart of Old Norse [[skirt]]; both mean a short garment, which brings [[shorts]] into the family.
The Old Norse version of Old English [[shirt]]; both mean a short garment, like [[shorts]].
In the same family as [[shirt]] and [[skirt]], which both mean a short garment.
Uses an old sense of hoot meaning the tiniest possible amount; nothing to do with owls.

entries.term: wouldn't touch with a ten-foot pole
entries.note: In the mid-1800s it was a 40-foot pole. A variant used a barge pole of 8 to 16 feet, and the Grinch's is 39½ feet.
Sleight of hand. The 19th-century French magician Jules de Rovère added 'digit' to Latin praestigiator, 'juggler, deceiver', giving it extra fingers.
From French sorcier, so Rob argues it should really just be 'sorcer'; Jess says English is working too hard.
The Old English plural was fishes; using the singular form as the plural is a Middle English invention.
Its cuttle means a bag or pouch and is probably related to [[cod]]; the animal belongs to the genus [[sepia]].
Latin for cuttlefish. In English it came to name the brown pigment once made from [[cuttlefish]] ink, hence sepia photo filters.
From medieval Latin dies mali, two unlucky days a month on calendars. It entered English as 'in the dismal', making 'dismal day' a tautology.
From Latin vinum, a very early borrowing into the Germanic languages that became English, taken directly from the Romans.
From Latin caseus, a very early borrowing into the Germanic languages that became English, taken directly from the Romans.
Not a garden where children play but a figurative garden where children grow like sweet little flowers.
A German military acronym for an anti-aircraft cannon. In WWII it extended to shells bursting around aircrews, and now means any criticism.
